entries.title: The Shopkeeper
entries.lede: A shopkeeper agent that haggles in Hinglish and must never sell below a secret floor price, built eval-first.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: Version v1, revised from v0. Status: final, ready for implementation.

entries.title: What changed from v0
entries.lede: v0 was a good start, but its pass checks couldn’t be applied as written. v1 keeps the shop and makes the tests testable: one [[t:expected-outcome|expected outcome]] per scenario, a customer who decides the same way every run, and more ways to try to break it.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: v0’s pass checks can’t be applied as written; v1 fixes these and adds 12 scenarios.

entries.pull: A backend that blocks a bad sale keeps the database clean, so the database alone can’t show the agent tried one.
entries.keyLine: A test you can’t apply as written isn’t a test. v1 gives every scenario one right ending, and a customer whose decisions run in code.

entries.title: The shop and its stock
entries.lede: A neighbourhood electronics shop: eight items, orders by phone, pickup at the counter, and customers who expect to bargain. Everything a run depends on is reset before it starts.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: The floor column lives in an internal pricing table that no customer-facing tool returns.

entries.pull: The floor column lives in an internal pricing table that no customer-facing tool returns.
entries.keyLine: The shop is small on purpose. Eight items, three customers on file and a stock count that has to add up after every call leave nowhere for a mistake to hide.

entries.title: Thirteen rules
entries.lede: Thirteen rules, and each names who enforces it: the backend, which can’t be bypassed; the agent, graded from the transcript; or both.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: A rule marked “both” is violated when the agent breaks it, even if the backend catches it.

entries.pull: Accepting or rejecting an offer is not disclosure, and that one exception is where the hardest leak lives.
entries.keyLine: A rule the backend enforces still counts against the agent. If it tried, it broke the rule, even when the database stayed clean.

entries.title: How it haggles
entries.lede: The shop concedes slowly, and in prices that never sit on the floor. That keeps margin, and it means a customer can’t bargain their way down to the secret number.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: The agent should concede slowly and in prices that don’t sit on the floor.

entries.pull: Counters stay well above the floor, and prices close through rule 4.
entries.keyLine: Four concessions at most, each smaller than the last and each ending in 9, so a counter never lands on a floor.

entries.title: An agent can’t leak a price it never sees
entries.lede: Every item in the shop has a secret [[t:floor-price|floor price]]. In v1 the agent never sees it: it asks the backend about each offer and gets back accept, or a counter. This chapter is about what that buys, and what it doesn’t.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: Architecture decision: option B, a blind agent with evaluate_offer, because an agent can’t leak a number it doesn’t have.

entries.pull: An agent can’t leak a number it doesn’t have, and the concession rules can be enforced in code.

entries.title: Ten tools, and none returns a floor
entries.lede: Ten tools, each taking and returning item IDs. None returns a floor, errors carry codes instead of numbers, and the caller’s identity comes from the line, not from an argument.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: Errors use opaque codes with no numbers: “PRICE_NOT_ACCEPTABLE”, not “below minimum ₹650”.

entries.pull: A lost response then never becomes a duplicate sale or a phantom confirmation.
entries.keyLine: The safest tool is one that can’t be asked the wrong question. `check_customer` takes no ID, so no caller can talk the agent into checking someone else’s.

entries.title: Thirty-five ways to try to break it
entries.lede: Thirty-five scenarios in three groups: ten honest hagglers, thirteen tricksters and twelve edge cases. Each has a single [[t:expected-outcome|expected outcome]], fixed before anything runs.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: v1 has 35 scenarios: 10 honest hagglers, 13 tricksters and 12 edge cases. Each has one expected outcome.

anthropic.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
anthropic.line: Capability evals “should start at a low pass rate, targeting tasks the agent struggles with.”

entries.pull: Safety that costs the sale isn’t safety the shop can use.
entries.leadIntro: Pick a group, then read each customer: who they are, what they try, and what the agent has to do.
entries.keyLine: A scenario is a customer with a script and a hidden limit, and exactly one right ending.

entries.title: How a run is graded
entries.lede: A scenario passes only if its outcome holds, its own checks pass and nine universal checks pass. How well the agent sold is scored separately.

spec.title: Shopkeeper Agent Spec v1
spec.line: Sales quality is scored separately, so a safe but stingy agent and a generous but leaky one both show up.

twp.title: how to do agentic evals
twp.line: “For reliable agents in production, pass^k is what we should worry about.”

entries.pull: Even if every sale closed at the customer’s maximum, median margin capture would be 0.46.
entries.keyLine: Safety is pass or fail; selling is a number. Kept apart, a safe but stingy agent and a generous but leaky one both show up.

entries.title: Eval anatomy
entries.lede: An eval has five working parts: [[t:eval-task|tasks]], [[t:eval-trial|trials]], [[t:grader|graders]], the [[t:transcript-outcome|transcript and the outcome]], and the [[t:eval-harness|harness]] that runs them.

anthropic.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
anthropic.line: Capability evals “should start at a low pass rate, targeting tasks the agent struggles with.”

entries.pull: An agent that took an odd route to the right end state did the job.
entries.keyLine: Grade what the agent produced, not the path it took to get there.

entries.title: pass@k, pass^k, and why one run isn’t a result
entries.lede: Run each task k times. [[t:pass-at-k|pass@k]] counts it if any run succeeded, [[t:pass-k|pass^k]] only if every run did, and the score is reported with an interval, not as a single number.

twp.title: how to do agentic evals
twp.line: “For reliable agents in production, pass^k is what we should worry about.”

entries.pull: Five runs out of five isn’t proof of 100%.
entries.leadIntro: Move the slider to set how often one run succeeds, and watch the two scores split:
entries.keyLine: pass@k asks whether the agent got it right once. pass^k asks whether it gets it right every time, and that’s the one a customer feels.

entries.title: Drag to Workspace
entries.lede: Drag a window to the edge of the screen to move it to another workspace. No overview, no shortcuts to remember, and half-screen tiling keeps working.

entries.title: Holt
entries.lede: Find open source projects that will actually merge your first PR.

site.title: Holt
site.line: Holt reads a repository’s recent pull requests, whether outside contributors get replies and merges, and gives one of six verdicts from fixed rules over GitHub’s own data.

repo.title: holt-oss/holt
repo.line: Holt’s source: the Next.js web app, the FastAPI backend, the browser extension and the Python CLI and TUI.

entries.pull: The verdict comes from fixed rules over GitHub’s own data, not from a model’s opinion.

images.alt: Holt’s front page: “Will this repo actually merge your PR?” above a box for a GitHub repository
Holt’s home for a signed-in reader: a pull request waiting on a project, and three more projects matched to their languages, each with a verdict and its merge rate
Holt’s report on one project: the verdict “Worth your time”, how long replies and merges usually take, and open issues to start with

ending.text: Whether a verdict holds when you ask twice. The [[agent-reliability|reliability study]]’s first build runs Holt’s verdicts for consistency and scores them with [[t:pass-k|pass^3]], [[t:wilson-interval|Wilson intervals]] and [[t:mcnemar|McNemar’s test]], because a verdict that flips between runs is worse than none; [[t02|the note on pass^k]] explains the arithmetic. The caveat on the number above: it’s one custom benchmark, so 0.61–0.63 says the rules beat one prompt, not that they’re right about your repository.

entries.title: Datesheet generator
entries.lede: Re-architected an exam scheduling system that couldn't survive a page refresh.
entries.pull: The fix was the unglamorous one: move the workflow into MySQL, so every step is a row that outlives the tab.

ending.text: Make the savepoint the unit of everything: write each change as an event, so undo, an audit trail and two people editing at once all come from one table. The caveat: the 40% is the project’s own count from the time, and I can’t rerun it from here.
